title: Set an impulse sprinkler's two trip collars so it waters only the quarter between two flags
instruction: Set the sprinkler so it waters only the bed between the two orange flags, then take your hands away.
context: The clicking impulse sprinkler on a spike is a fixture of American front lawns and parks, and anyone who has used one has had to stop it soaking the driveway, the sidewalk or the house: on an impulse sprinkler the watered arc is set by sliding two friction trip collars round the bearing under the head, one for each side of the arc, and the head's trip lever strikes them and reverses the head (Rain Bird's guide: plastic models' collars "move by just a push of the thumb"). Anyone can judge the result by watching one sweep. The collars sit under the head's drive arm and nozzle, so a hand has to come in low, under the free-turning head, and slide each collar's small tab a precise amount with a fingertip.
setup: Positions in cm from the arm bases' midpoint in x (forward) and the table's centre line in y (+y toward the left arm); headings in degrees about the sprinkler's axis, 0 pointing straight away from the robot, counter-clockwise seen from above. A green synthetic turf mat, 30 x 38 cm and 10 mm thick, lies on the table (x 16 to 46, y -19 to 19). At (27, 0) a plastic impulse sprinkler (the size of a Rain Bird P5R: 111 mm long, 114 mm tall; head 0.15 kg) stands on a steel spike whose 21 mm upright rises 30 mm above the turf. Its stationary bearing is a black plastic nut (26 mm across, 14 mm tall) and a sleeve (21 mm across, 25 mm tall) carrying two black plastic friction trip collars: each a ring 31 mm across and 8 mm tall with a tab 6 mm wide reaching 30 mm from the axis, the lower collar 17-25 mm and the upper 27-35 mm above the bearing's bottom. A collar turns on the sleeve only when pushed with 0.04 N m (1.3 N at the tab's end). The head turns on the bearing against 0.005 N m: a black plastic column 30 mm across, a nozzle barrel 12 mm across pointing forward and 25 degrees up, a drive arm on top with a plastic spoon at the nozzle end and a steel counterweight at the other (111 mm end to end), and a steel trip lever 4 mm wide hanging behind the column, opposite the nozzle, beside both tabs. With the water on the head turns until its lever meets a tab, then reverses, so it waters the arc between the collars on the side away from them. Two marker flags (white plastic posts 6 mm across and 11 cm tall, each with an orange 40 x 28 mm flag) stand on the turf 24 cm from the sprinkler at headings -45 and +45: the bed to water is the quarter between them, away from the robot. At the start the nozzle points at -23, the lower collar's tab at 53 and the upper's at 307: the sprinkler waters 220 degrees, from -110 to +110. Both grippers start open at the ready pose. The screenshot shows the start.
scoring: The sweep's ends are the nozzle's headings where the head reverses, its trip lever against a collar's tab. Readings start once the robot has reached in and then both grippers have been 17 cm or more from the sprinkler's axis (or 6.5 cm above the head's top) and still for 2 s; a gripper coming back within that shuts the water off and the readings start again. Each end earns 1 within 10 degrees of its flag's heading (-45 for the clockwise end, +45 for the counter-clockwise end), 0.5 within 20, 0.25 within 30, otherwise 0; the score is the mean of the two ends, once each end has been reached (the latest reading each way counts). No readings (the robot never parks clear and still) scores 0, and so does doing nothing: the ends stay at -110 and +110, 65 degrees off each. Real trial: the water stays off; the supervisor turns the head slowly by hand, one way and then the other, until the lever touches a tab (a fingertip touch, not pushing through), and reads the nozzle's heading on a printed 360-degree disc taped to the turf round the spike (1-degree marks), with an overhead photo of each reading. Simulation: water is a scripted velocity drive that turns the head at 20 deg/s with at most 0.015 N m from 2 s after the grippers are parked and reverses it after 0.1 s stalled; each reversal's heading is recorded.
reset_notes: Nothing is consumed. Turn the head to point at -23 and slide the lower collar's tab to 53 and the upper's to 307 on the printed disc; spring-scale test: each collar slips at 1.3 N (plus or minus 0.3 N) pulled at its tab's end, and the head turns at 0.2 N or less pulled at its nozzle tip. The spike and turf mat stay on their taped outlines.
fidelity: Rigid parts on one articulation with Coulomb joint friction. Water is not simulated: a scripted drive turns the head and reverses it when its rigid trip lever stalls against a tab (a real head steps round on its drive arm and its lever toggles). The head's overall size is the catalog's; part widths, collar and tab sizes, masses and the collars' slip torque are estimates. No spray, springs or stream.
scores: Scripted open-loop demo: 1.0 in four simulator runs (three cloud, one local). Dream-1 run: 0.0.
